prompt: Which of the six questions decides most choices of store on its own?
hint: It is asked first.

choices.text: What it costs
choices.why: Price is asked last, once the workload says what to multiply.

choices.text: The access pattern
choices.why: Right: how the data is written and read.

choices.text: Who runs the store and how many stores the team already operates
choices.why: It matters, fifth, after the shape of the workload.

choices.text: How big the data grows over the next three years
choices.why: Size is the fourth question; the pattern decides the branch first.

prompt: A dashboard of yesterday's sales and a customer who has just paid both read orders. Which question separates them most clearly?
hint: Must the read see the latest write?

choices.text: Scale
choices.why: Both are small; the difference is in what each needs to see.

choices.text: Who runs it
choices.why: The same team runs both.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Right. The customer needs their own write; the dashboard may be a day behind.

choices.text: The price of the storage both read from
choices.why: Price comes after the reader's needs are known.

prompt: Asked first, why does the price question pick a serverless SQL pool for the "my orders" screen?
hint: Compare billed per hour with billed per terabyte, before the volume is known.

choices.text: Billed per terabyte, it looks cheaper than a database billed every hour, until the lookups are counted
choices.why: Right. At three million lookups of 10 MB minimum, it was 150 USD and seconds per lookup.

choices.text: Because it is the fastest store for lookups by key
choices.why: It takes seconds per query; a screen cannot wait.

choices.text: It holds the orders already
choices.why: The lake's copy is derived; the store of record is the SQL database.

choices.text: Because Cosmos DB is not available in brazilsouth
choices.why: Nothing in the course says so; the lessons used brazilsouth throughout.

prompt: A team of three already runs Azure SQL Database. Which question asks them to count that before adding Cosmos DB for one small feature?
hint: Every store has work that does not go away.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Both stores can give the feature what it needs to read.

choices.text: Who runs it
choices.why: Right. A new store is a new set of failures to learn at three in the morning.

choices.text: Latency, because Cosmos DB is slower
choices.why: Read by key, Cosmos DB answers in milliseconds.

choices.text: The access pattern, because small features have none
choices.why: Every workload has an access pattern; this question is about operations.

prompt: Match each workload to the branch of the tree it falls in.
hint: The access pattern decides.

pairs.left: A customer's cart, by the customer id
An order and its stock update, all or nothing
Tax records kept for years and rarely read
Revenue by neighbourhood over two years

prompt: Why does the tree draw the cache beside the database rather than as a branch of its own?
hint: Where does the data live?

choices.text: Redis cannot store more than a few gigabytes
choices.why: Size is not the reason given.

choices.text: It only holds copies
choices.why: Right. It is never the branch on its own.

choices.text: Caches are slower than databases for single items
choices.why: They answer in under a millisecond; speed is their purpose.

choices.text: Because the cache is the subject of another course
choices.why: Lesson 15 of this course teaches it.

prompt: Quitanda's orders are written in transactions and analysed over two years. What does the lesson do with such a workload?
hint: Two branches.

choices.text: Treats it as two workloads: the order in SQL, a derived copy in the lake
choices.why: Right, kept current by a pipeline or a change stream.

choices.text: Puts everything in Synapse, which does both
choices.why: A warehouse is not built for a checkout's transactions.

choices.text: Runs the analysts' scans on the checkout database
choices.why: That is the anti-pattern of one store for everything: every sale slows at noon.

choices.text: Writes each order to SQL and to the lake from the shop
choices.why: Two stores accepting writes for one fact become two truths.

prompt: Where do events from Event Hubs end up, in the tree's terms?
hint: A stream is a way in.

choices.text: In Event Hubs, which keeps them as history
choices.why: Retention is days, not history.

choices.text: In a store of another branch
choices.why: Right: Cosmos DB for the latest state, the lake for history.

choices.text: In the cache, until somebody reads them
choices.why: A cache is not where a stream lands for keeping.

choices.text: Nowhere; they are read and dropped
choices.why: What arrives is read by a job and lands in a store.

prompt: Which consistency level does the lesson give Quitanda's carts in Cosmos DB, and why?
hint: The default of lesson 12.

choices.text: Strong, because carts are money
choices.why: A cart needs the customer to see their own change, which session gives at lower cost.

choices.text: Eventual, because carts are abandoned anyway
choices.why: A customer who adds an item and does not see it is a lost sale.

choices.text: Session: a customer always sees their own last change
choices.why: Right, which is exactly what a cart needs.

choices.text: Bounded staleness of one day
choices.why: A day behind would show yesterday's cart.

prompt: Why is the product page served from Azure Cache for Redis rather than straight from SQL?
hint: Read often, changed rarely.

choices.text: Many reads, few changes
choices.why: Right. The cache answers the reads; SQL stays the store of record.

choices.text: SQL cannot store product descriptions
choices.why: It can; the point is how often they are read.

choices.text: Redis keeps the prices consistent
choices.why: A cache is behind its source; the time to live bounds how far.

choices.text: Redis is cheaper per gigabyte stored
choices.why: Memory is dear; the reason is latency.

prompt: The analysts' hourly dashboard is now refreshed by thirty people all day, over the lake with a serverless pool. What does the lesson say to revisit?
hint: Per query against per hour.

choices.text: The lake's layout, because Delta is too slow
choices.why: The layout matters for any engine; the point here is how the engine is billed.

choices.text: Per-hour capacity versus per-query cost
choices.why: Right. The volume the access pattern produces changed the price answer.

choices.text: Moving the dashboard to Cosmos DB
choices.why: Scans and aggregates are the warehouse branch, not lookups by key.

choices.text: Nothing; serverless is always the cheapest
choices.why: Per-query billing loses at high, steady volume.

prompt: What is the rule that keeps two copies of an order from becoming two truths?
hint: Only one place accepts the write.

choices.text: Write every copy in the same transaction
choices.why: Across stores there is no such transaction, which is lesson 24's point.

choices.text: Compare the copies every night and keep the newer
choices.why: Newer is not necessarily right; there is no way to say which is.

choices.text: One store of record per fact, the others derived
choices.why: Right. The derived copies can be rebuilt from the record.

choices.text: Keep only one copy of any data
choices.why: Copies are fine and necessary; the rule is about which one is written to.

prompt: In `compare.py`, Cosmos DB's request units cost 3.15 USD. If a lookup really costs 9 request units instead of 3, and writes stay at 6, what do the request units cost, in USD?
Why does the Azure SQL Database line read differently if the orders already live there for the checkout?
hint: What is the price made of?

choices.text: The machine is already paid for
choices.why: Right. 365 of the 371 is the two vCores, billed whether the screen is opened or not.

choices.text: Because a second database is billed at half price
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's arithmetic says so.

choices.text: Storage would then be free
choices.why: Storage is 6.00 either way; it is the compute that is shared.

choices.text: SQL lookups become slower when shared
choices.why: With an index, the lookup is fast; the question is cost.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the serverless SQL pool is the wrong shape "at any price"?
hint: Two problems, one of which no price fixes.

choices.text: It charges a minimum of 10 MB per query
choices.why: That makes it dear here, which a lower price could fix; the other problem cannot be.

choices.text: Each lookup takes seconds
choices.why: Right. Latency rules it out before price is read.

choices.text: It cannot read Delta files
choices.why: Lessons 16 and 17 have the lake engines reading Delta in place.

choices.text: It is not available for less than a terabyte of data
choices.why: There is no such floor; the minimum is per query.

prompt: At the lesson's 10 MB minimum per query and an illustrative 5.00 USD per TB, what would 600,000 lookups a month cost on the serverless pool, in USD?
hint: 600,000 × 10 MB in TB, times 5.

prompt: A `jobs` table in Azure SQL Database, polled every second by ten workers. What goes wrong as it grows?
hint: A database built for transactions, used for delivery.

choices.text: SQL refuses more than one reader per table
choices.why: It accepts them; they fight over the same rows with locks.

choices.text: Lock fights and idle load
choices.why: Right. A queue or Event Hubs delivers without polling.

choices.text: The rows are lost when a worker crashes
choices.why: The rows stay; the problems are contention and load.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the table has an index
choices.why: An index helps the poll; it does not remove the locks or the polling.

prompt: A Cosmos DB container is partitioned by a field nobody queries on. What is the fix the lesson names?
hint: A bigger throughput setting is not it.

choices.text: Raising the throughput until queries are fast
choices.why: Every query still crosses every partition, and the charge grows with the data.

choices.text: Adding an index on every field
choices.why: Cosmos DB indexes everything by default; the partitions are the problem.

choices.text: Re-partition by the right field, in a new container
choices.why: Right, which means a migration; the key cannot be changed in place.

choices.text: Moving the queries to a serverless SQL pool
choices.why: That trades one wrong shape for another.

prompt: Quitanda's carts are written only to Redis, with no database behind them. A failover drops some keys. Whose fault is it?
hint: What does a cache promise?

choices.text: Redis, which lost acknowledged writes by a bug
choices.why: Losing keys on eviction or failover is allowed by design for a cache.

choices.text: Whoever chose a cache as the record
choices.why: Right. A cache holds copies; carts might tolerate it, orders could not.

choices.text: Azure, which should have kept a backup
choices.why: What a tier persists is documented; relying on more is the design's choice.

choices.text: The application, which read too often
choices.why: Reading does not drop keys.

prompt: A partition key such as today's date sends all of today's writes to one partition, which is called a ___ partition.
hint: It is the opposite of cold.

prompt: Put the six questions in the order the lesson asks them.
hint: Price is last.
items: How fast must an answer come?
What consistency does the reader need?
How big, and how fast does it grow?
What does it cost, at this workload?

prompt: Which of these are true of `compare.py`? Choose all that apply.
hint: What did it ask, and what are its numbers?

choices.text: Its prices are illustrative, not Azure's
choices.why: Right; the price sheet of lesson 1 gives real ones.

choices.text: Its request units per lookup are an estimate to replace with a measurement
choices.why: Right; Azure's request charge header gives the real figure.

choices.text: It queried the Cosmos DB emulator for its request charges
choices.why: It asks nothing; the emulator's flat charge would teach nothing anyway.

choices.text: It proves Cosmos DB is the cheapest store for every workload
choices.why: It priced one workload, whose pattern is Cosmos DB's branch.

prompt: A new feature shows each customer how many times they ordered each product in the last two years, refreshed once a night. Where does the lesson's reasoning put it?
hint: Two workloads: computing it and showing it.

choices.text: Run the two-year count on the checkout database each time the screen opens
choices.why: A scan on the store of record at every opening is the one-store anti-pattern.

choices.text: Query the lake with a serverless pool from the screen
choices.why: Seconds per lookup and a 10 MB minimum each, as the lesson priced.

choices.text: Nightly over the lake, served from Cosmos DB
choices.why: Right. The scan is the warehouse branch, the screen the key branch.

choices.text: Keep the counts only in Redis
choices.why: A cache is not a store of record; a failover would lose them.
